# Field Guide to 287(g)

## for journalists

# What it covers:

This is a practical guide for local reporters, investigative journalists, and independent media seeking public records related to ICE’s 287(g) program and its implementation at participating agencies. It assumes you already know the basics of how the 287(g) program works — to learn more before diving into this guide, [see here](https://www.tituslegaldesign.com/immigration-101/287g-program) (and stay tuned for more resources).

It covers four things: 

* a breakdown of ICE's layered contract chain, and what each layer reveals (see ‘[Document Chain]()’);

* understanding the specific legal language that ICE uses across its multilayered contract system (see ‘[ICE Contract Language]()’);

* how to send federal FOIA requests to ICE, and what you can realistically expect in response (see ‘[Federal FOIA]()’);

* what to include for county and municipal records requests (see ‘[State \+ Local Records]()’) and the documents that have been produced from similar requests (see ‘[Resources \+ References]()’).

It does ***not*** include fill-in-the-blank template letters, primarily because of the wide variation in format, length \+ content requirements, etc. across government agencies. Instead, I’ve focused this guide on what to ask for, where to look, and how to frame your requests.

---

**NOT Legal Advice:** This guide is reporting guidance, not legal advice, and its author is **not a lawyer**. Public records law varies by state and changes often — any specific statutes, deadlines, or other regulations cited here should always be independently verified for currency \+ accuracy.

---

# 

# tl;dr

Do *not* start with ICE. Start with the participating agency and, when applicable, the municipal or county government that authorized the agreement (see ‘[Authorization Process]()’). The sheriff's office or police department, the town/county auditor, or the town council/county board hold the same (or similar) contract documents and reimbursement requests \+ payment records.

ICE's own agreement instructs partner agencies to clear disclosures with ICE first — but it also contains a carve-out preserving state public records compliance, and it expressly authorizes agencies to give the signed agreement to the media upon request.

---

Update from the American Immigration Council (**August 11, 2026**):

“ICE has been telling local governments that partner with the agency what they can and can’t release to the public, even under their own state laws. The Dallas Morning News [reported](https://www.dallasnews.com/news/politics/article/ice-texas-public-records-states-rights-secrecy-22291873.php) that in April, ICE emailed jurisdictions with 287(g) agreements, asserting that the “prohibition on \[an\] agency’s unilateral release of ICE information is expansive” and ordered them to “immediately consult with the ICE FOIA office, ICE Public Affairs, or your local Field Office Director” before responding to any public records requests. 

Although these directives were sent in April, local law enforcement agencies were already blocking access to records under state law. Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC) and Professor Meghan Conley requested records from certain Tennessee county jails temporarily housing people in detention on ICE’s behalf, including basic records that county jails routinely create for all detainees. The jails refused, at ICE’s direction.”

“Even if the documents were available from ICE, the federal FOIA is not an adequate alternative. ICE often ignores FOIA requests, all too often releasing records only after requesters sue the agency in federal court. Not all requesters have the resources to do so, and litigation often takes months.

“[ICE Is Trying to Hide State Records of People in Detention. We Filed a FOIA to Find Out Why](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/blog/ice-hide-state-records-people-in-detention-foia/)” by **Meghan Conley** (Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition), and **Raul Pinto** (American Immigration Council)

# 287(g) Program Overview

*As of: August 2026*

[Scale](#scale)

[Money](#money)

[Capacity and oversight](#capacity-and-oversight)

[Legal pressure and local accountability](#legal-pressure-and-local-accountability)

## **Scale** {#scale}

ICE reported 2,179 signed Memoranda of Agreement as of July 20th, 2026, across 39 states and two U.S. territories. 

In January 2025 the figure was 135\. That is roughly a 16-fold expansion in roughly 18 months. And the expansion is overwhelmingly concentrated in the Task Force Model — the version that places immigration enforcement authority into routine street policing, and the version that was suspended in 2012 after federal findings of racial profiling. It’s also the version that’s now tied to a range of financial incentives for participating agencies.

**See the Report:** [Active 287(g) Agreements](https://datastudio.google.com/reporting/ebe8be08-53be-4afc-9240-83ec3075e873)

---

## **Money** {#money}

Before October 2025, DHS only covered training costs and limited software expenses related to agencies’ participation in the program. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) changed that, and ICE began marketing vehicle grants, technology subscriptions, officer payroll and overtime, and quota-based bonuses to Task Force partners.

For more on the financial incentives involved, see ‘[The Money]()’ section.

**Note**: The original DHS announcement re: 287(g) financial reimbursement incentives, posted September 02, 2025, appears to have been removed in July 2026\. Here is the Wayback Machine archive:

[https\://web.archive.org/web/20260714100549/https\://www\.dhs.gov/news/2025/09/02/dhs-announces-new-reimbursement-opportunities-state-and-local-law-enforcement](https://web.archive.org/web/20260714100549/https://www.dhs.gov/news/2025/09/02/dhs-announces-new-reimbursement-opportunities-state-and-local-law-enforcement)

---

## **Capacity and oversight** {#capacity-and-oversight}

DHS said in [September 2025](https://web.archive.org/web/20260714100549/https://www.dhs.gov/news/2025/09/02/dhs-announces-new-reimbursement-opportunities-state-and-local-law-enforcement) that it had trained or was training more than 10,000 officers under the Task Force Model, while [reducing training requirements](https://forumtogether.org/article/explainer-training-under-the-revived-287g-task-force-model/) and expanding supervisory \+ vetting capacity slower than the program’s expansion would otherwise require. A 2010 DHS Office of Inspector General report [found deficiencies](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/dhs-report-confirms-serious-civil-rights-problems-local-immigration-enforcement) (ACLU) in oversight and training and concluded the program lacks adequate safeguards against racial profiling. 

**See also:**

[DHS Inspector General announces pending investigations into ICE, CBP \| Immigration Policy Tracking Project](https://immpolicytracking.org/policies/dhs-inspector-general-launches-investigations-into-ice-cbp/#/tab-policy-documents) (February 2026\)

[Letter from Ranking Member Peters to DHS General Counsel \- Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs](https://www.hsgac.senate.gov/library/files/letter-from-ranking-member-peters-to-dhs-general-counsel/) (March 2026\) 

---

## **Legal pressure and local accountability** {#legal-pressure-and-local-accountability}

The program is being challenged on multiple fronts, including civil rights litigation over stops and detention, [public records battles \+ litigation](#notable-/-ongoing-litigation), and challenges to whether officials at participating agencies even had authority to sign up.

A caution about counts. ICE publishes a snapshot that replaces its predecessor. Any figure is true only for the day it was captured, and agreements disappear without notice — though the MOA *technically* provides that ICE will publish a termination decision 90 days in advance.

## **‘BIDEN’ Grant (DOJ):**  {#‘biden’-grant-(doj):}

The OBBBA also authorized a \$3 billion [DOJ grant program](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/24/nx-s1-5886181/justice-department-is-offering-billions-in-new-grants-for-police-who-partner-with-ice) for law enforcement agencies, with eligibility tied to 287(g) participation (and/or other federal task force program), and with [multiple application rounds](https://bja.ojp.gov/funding/opportunities/DOJ-FY26-BIDEN-program). 

See [§61101. Bridging Immigration-related Deficits Experienced Nationwide Reimbursement Fund](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title34-section61101&num=0&edition=prelim).

---

## **State Grants** {#state-grants}

Several states run parallel state-level grant programs. My program report includes a separate tracking of state-level grant awards, totaling over \$62 million in confirmed grants (and over \$330 million earmarked)  across just three states:

* **Tennessee**, through a [\$75 million grant program](https://newschannel9.com/news/local/new-documents-show-how-hamilton-county-training-center-287g-program-came-together) for county sheriffs, managed by the state’s Office of Criminal Justice Programs.  
  * eligibility requires the agency to demonstrate it “has taken all necessary steps to enter into a 287(g) agreement with the federal government.”  
  * see [Grant Solicitation Packet](https://newschannel9.com/resources/pdf/458d91d2-d0ae-421f-bb32-e61b31cd1e02-FY26VCIFZipCodesTnGrants.pdf), published by WTVC (May 22, 2026\)

* **Texas**, through the state [comptroller’s office, under SB 8](https://comptroller.texas.gov/economy/development/grants/sb8/).   
  * Full details \+ documentation on the [Sheriff Immigration Law Enforcement Grant Program](https://comptroller.texas.gov/economy/development/grants/)

* **Florida** through its [State Board of Immigration Enforcement](https://myfloridacfo.com/news/pressreleases/press-release-details/2026/07/23/chief-financial-officer-blaise-ingoglia-awards-over--8.5-million-to-strengthen-local-law-enforcement-capabilities) (SBIE)  
  * \$250+ million earmarked for SBIE grants

**See: \$ [State Grant Records](https://datastudio.google.com/s/vMxaqun25LA)**

# Document chain {#document-chain}

[Layer 0: ICE Active Agreement List](#layer-0:-ice-active-agreement-list)

[Layer 1: Memorandum of Agreement](#layer-1:-memorandum-of-agreement)

[Layer 2: Service Agreement](#layer-2:-service-agreement)

[Layer 3: Incentives Attachment(s)](#layer-3:-incentives-attachment\(s\))

[Layer 4: Reimbursement requests and payment/performance records](#layer-4:-reimbursement-requests-and-payment/performance-records)

[Layer 5: Program data and authorization file](#layer-5:-program-data-and-authorization-file)

[Tip: Follow the document trail](#tip:-follow-the-document-trail)

**Document Layers:** ICE's 287(g) partnerships are governed and managed by a layered contract that obscures the details behind the agreements’ scope of authority, financial incentives, expectations and requirements for participating agencies, etc.

---

## **Layer 0: ICE Active Agreement List**  {#layer-0:-ice-active-agreement-list}

An Excel spreadsheet available for download on [ICE's 287(g) program page](https://www.ice.gov/identify-and-arrest/287g); updated irregularly and without announcement.

**Versioning note:**  Each version of the spreadsheet replaces the previous one entirely. There is no changelog, no archive, and no unique identifier for any agreement.

**Tells you:** who is participating, under which model, and the ICE signature date\*. 

**\*Note:** the participating agency official’s signature date (i.e. the date they submitted their application to ICE ERO), is  often a day or two earlier and only verifiable in Layer 1 (see below).

**Does not tell you:** details on scope of authority and agreement terms, money, signatories, or canceled agreement metadata.

---

## **Layer 1: Memorandum of Agreement** {#layer-1:-memorandum-of-agreement}

The instrument that establishes the partnership. ICE publishes a blank [fillable template](https://www.ice.gov/identify-and-arrest/287g) for each of the 3 program models. The templates are boilerplate, and primarily set  out delegated authority, training requirements, and program-related supervision in general terms. It contains no reference to the UAC safety verification initiative or dollar figures.

**Where to get it:** ICE's published agreement list (Layer 0\) includes a link to each signed MOA published by ICE. 

However, these document links are typically added **2-3 weeks** *after* the agreement first appears on ICE’s  spreadsheet. You’ll see ‘*link pending*’ in the MOA column for new agreements.

**Use it for:** confirming the signature date against the published list — they disagree more often than you might expect (and please let me know of any inaccuracies [in my report](https://www.tituslegaldesign.com/immigration-101/287g-report-methodology)\!)

---

## **Layer 2: Service Agreement** {#layer-2:-service-agreement}

Agency-specific, signed by the sheriff, police chief, etc. and not proactively released by anyone. 

This is the layer that expands the scope of the partnership beyond what the MOA describes — including work locating minors formerly in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody — and sets the reporting obligations that generate the paper trail in Layer 4\.

**Get it from:** the participating agency.  The first one to surface publicly came from an Idaho sheriff's office via [*InvestigateWest* in April 2026\.](https://www.investigatewest.org/rural-idaho-sheriffs-office-got-at-least-116-000-for-helping-ice/)

---

## **Layer 3: Incentives Attachment(s)** {#layer-3:-incentives-attachment(s)}

A rider referenced by the service agreement, but not signed by either party. This is where the money is specified: a schedule of per-case payments tied to categories of completed work. 

Because it is unsigned, agencies sometimes argue it is not a contract document. It is incorporated by reference, which is why the service agreement points at it.

**Get it from:** the participating agency, or occasionally a state grant administrator. The known copy surfaced through the [*Chattanooga Times Free Press* reporting on Bradley County, Tennessee constables](https://www.timesfreepress.com/news/2026/jul/12/tennessee-constable-could-see-394k-from-ice/).

---

## **Layer 4: Reimbursement requests and payment/performance records** {#layer-4:-reimbursement-requests-and-payment/performance-records}

Invoices and reimbursement requests submitted to ICE, payments received. Budget amendments to accept federal funds into local accounts. Purchase orders for vehicles, body cameras, surveillance software or database access subscriptions. Officer overtime and travel records. Training certifications. Board agenda packets and minutes from the meeting where the agreement was approved.

This layer is generated locally, held locally, and often duplicated across multiple local offices. It’s also the layer most likely to answer the question ICE has not: what ‘work’ has actually been done, and what was actually paid for it.

**Get it from:** the participating agency, the county auditor or city comptroller, county commission or town council, or a state grant administrator. It depends\!

---

## **Layer 5: Program data and authorization file** {#layer-5:-program-data-and-authorization-file}

Two categories the MOA itself guarantees exist:

1. **Program statistics:** § XII makes the agency responsible for tracking and maintaining accurate data on its own 287(g) program;  
2. **Authorization record:** the governing body's minutes, resolutions, and legal opinions, or the absence of them. 

**Get it from:** the agency, the government clerk, or the governing body (board, council, etc.). 

---

## **Tip: Follow the document trail** {#tip:-follow-the-document-trail}

One document can exist in several places, held by officials with different expectations and reporting obligations. A sheriff who stalls on a request for their service agreement may have already submitted the same document to the county commission as an agenda attachment, to the county auditor as standard financial procedure, or to the state comptroller as part of a grant application. 

---

# 

# ICE's contract language

[Contract Vocabulary \+ Common Language](#contract-vocabulary-+-common-language)

[Specific Contract Language](#specific-contract-language)

The 287(g) documents are written in government procurement language, which can obscure what is actually being described. All terms and clauses referenced below come from the Task Force Model MOA revision dated **August 19, 2025** — check the revision date on any copy you obtain for versioning purposes.

---

## **Contract Vocabulary \+ Common Language** {#contract-vocabulary-+-common-language}

| ‘service provider’ | The participating law enforcement agency (LEA). Reframes the agency as a vendor delivering a contracted service to a federal customer — in this case, that’s ICE / DHS. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **‘credentialed TFO’** | A Task Force Officer (TFO) is any LEO employed by an agency participating in the Task Force Model 287(g), who has completed ICE's online training and is authorized to act on ICE’s behalf.  Reporting obligations are tied to each credentialed officer, which would imply participating agencies are documenting per-officer records of TFO-invoiced hours somewhere. |
| **‘apprehension’** | Used in the service agreement's reporting clause. Note where it appears and where it doesn’t — like the UAC incentives document, which describes the same work with different language. |
| **‘safety verification’** | The UAC incentives document uses this term to describe locating a minor and confirming their living situation and school enrollment. **Not an arrest**. The gap between this phrase and "apprehension"in the service agreement is important, and it may be worth quoting both rather than paraphrasing them. |
| **‘Unaccompanied alien children’ (UAC)** | ICE's statutory term. Definitionally narrowed in the service agreement to cases "specifically designated by ICE" — meaning ICE controls which children are on the list, and the list itself is **not public**. |
| **‘unaccounted for’** | Does not mean missing. It means released from federal custody and not currently tracked by the agency. Officials have used the ambiguity to imply the former. |
| **‘incentive’ / ‘reimbursement’ /  ‘grant‘** | Three different things, but conflated in usage. A reimbursement repays a documented cost;  a grant is awarded upfront against a budget (in this case, largely through state boards \+ state comptroller grant programs); and an incentive is paid on completion of an outcome (in this case, quota-based financial bonuses for certain Task Force program work, like the UAC Safety Verification Incentive (see below). |
| **‘incorporated by reference**’ | Pulls an external document into the contract without reproducing it. This is the hinge that makes an unsigned attachment binding — like the [UAC Safety Verification Incentives](https://wehco.media.clients.ellingtoncms.com/news/document/2026/07/10/CTFP-UAC_Safety_Verification_Initiative_Incentives_Program_for_287g_Partners.pdf) document — and a phrase to consider searching for when you suspect another contract layer may exist. |

---

## **Specific Contract Language** {#specific-contract-language}

Passages from the documents that have surfaced, as quoted:

1. **Scope of UAC work** — [287(g) service agreement](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28083186-287g-service-agreement-ocso-2/), Owyhee County Sheriff's Office (Idaho):

   1. "any case specifically designated by ICE that was previously in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody, subsequently released, and unaccounted for."

2. **Reporting obligation** — same [287(g) service agreement](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28083186-287g-service-agreement-ocso-2/):

   1. "The service provider shall provide ERO with hours spent performing ICE enforcement activities for adult and Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC), for each credentialed TFO assigned to the apprehension."

3. [**UAC Safety Verification Initiative,** Incentives Program for 287(g) Partners](https://wehco.media.clients.ellingtoncms.com/news/document/2026/07/10/CTFP-UAC_Safety_Verification_Initiative_Incentives_Program_for_287g_Partners.pdf):

   1. "Two incentive categories are available to agencies participating in the initiative. When combined, they amount to \$22,500 in incentives per UAC case, depending on the scope of the work activities completed for each UAC case."

   2. The incentive total includes up to \$2,500 in "case incentives" for address verification and residence confirmation, and up to \$20,000 in "safety verification" incentives for what is referred to as more comprehensive safety and welfare verification activities.

# Authorization process

[What we’ve learned](#what-we’ve-learned)

[What to ask for](#what-to-ask-for)

We’ve learned of a growing number of agencies that appear to have joined the program either without proper authorization or outside the scope of their official capacity.

In several cases, the 287(g) MOA appears to have been signed by the sheriff or police chief without going through the formal authorization process, as set by the jurisdiction’s governing body, like the county board of commissioners or the city/town council. 

---

**Notes:**

* Consider how this authorization may be subject to state administrative procedures (see [Wyoming, below](https://www.aclu-wy.org/news/public-records-requests-result-in-inconsistent-authorization-of-287g-across-wyoming/)). 

* The absence of a documented authorization process does not automatically make an agreement unlawful. This requires local and state-level research to confirm authorization and reporting requirements — consider how the jurisdiction typically manages binding intergovernmental agreements that obligates funds or assumes new liability.  

* States also distribute authority between sheriffs and county boards differently, with some sheriffs holding independent constitutional authority

---

## **What we’ve learned** {#what-we’ve-learned}

**Wyoming:** After [suing Laramie County](https://www.aclu-wy.org/cases/juntos-et-al-v-kozak/), the ACLU of Wyoming filed records requests with the seven other counties holding active agreements and with the Wyoming Highway Patrol, seeking proof of governing-body approval and of compliance with the Wyoming Administrative Procedures Act. 

* [The responses](https://live-awp-wyoming.pantheonsite.io/app/uploads/2026/07/ORR-Responses.pdf), published in July 2026, are revealing:  
  * Campbell, Hot Springs, Lincoln, and Natrona counties couldn’t produce any  records to show the agreements were ever considered or approved by their commissioners.  
  * Carbon County did sanction participation, after a 2025 presentation from its sheriff.  
  * Crook County relies on a 1998 resolution granting the sheriff blanket authority to enter agreements with other law enforcement agencies.  
  * Sweetwater County passed a resolution in early July 2026 retroactively ratifying every agreement its former sheriff had entered with ICE since 2020\.

* ZERO of the responding agencies were able to provide any record of state administrative rulemaking compliance.

More on the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office: [https\://www\.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/06/12/us/politics/ice-local-police-immigration-287g](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/06/12/us/politics/ice-local-police-immigration-287g)

---

**Montana:** Four Gallatin County residents sued the county and sheriff in April 2026 over a 2020 agreement the commission never ratified. The county agreed to suspend 287(g) operations pending a ratification vote at a public hearing in July 2026\.

[County ICE agreement fails amid prevailing statute](https://www.bozemandailychronicle.com/townnews/legislation/county-ice-agreement-fails-amid-prevailing-statute/article_25dc5b04-73ce-4543-8a51-a60095774e4b.html) (Bozeman Daily Chronicle, June 2026\)

---

**Arizona:** Outside counsel retained by Pinal County concluded in a January 2026 opinion that the county's agreement was void for lack of Board of Supervisors approval. The supervisors subsequently authorized legal action.

[‘Determined to be void:’ Judge rules against Pinal County Attorney contract with ICE](https://news.azpm.org/p/azpmnews/2026/5/28/229921-determined-to-be-void-judge-rules-against-pinal-county-attorney-contract-with-ice/) (AZPM, May 2026\)

[Judge blocks Pinal County Attorney's rogue ICE deal, says he exceeded his authority](https://azmirror.com/2026/05/15/judge-blocks-pinal-county-attorneys-rogue-ice-deal-says-he-exceeded-his-authority/) (AZ Mirror, May 2026\)

---

**Pennsylvania:** In [Make the Road Pennsylvania v. Harran](https://www.aclupa.org/cases/make-the-road-pennsylvania-v-harran/), the ACLU of Pennsylvania and the Community Justice Project challenged a Bucks County agreement signed without commissioner authorization. The trial court ruled for the sheriff on standing, finding no harm from an agreement not yet in effect. The sheriff then lost reelection; his successor ended the agreement in January 2026\. The appeal continues in Superior Court, with America First Legal defending. 

[Judge sides with Bucks county sheriffs over ICE agreement \- WHYY](https://whyy.org/articles/bucks-county-sheriff-ice-agreement-judge-ruling/) (October 2025\)

[New Bucks County sheriff Danny Ceisler sworn-in as debate over ICE enforcement in communities continues \- 6abc Philadelphia](https://6abc.com/post/new-bucks-county-sheriff-danny-ceisler-sworn-debate-ice-enforcement-communities-continues/18370588/) (January 2026\)

## 

## **What to ask for** {#what-to-ask-for}

* minutes, agendas, and any resolution of the governing body referencing the agreement, ICE, or immigration enforcement, for a window around the signature date; 

* any legal opinion from the county attorney or outside counsel on the agency signatory’s authority to sign; 

* any filing made under the state administrative procedure act (if applicable);

* any blanket or standing delegation of this intergovernmental contracting authority to the agency signatory;

* any resolution ratifying agreements after the fact.

# Federal FOIA: What to expect from ICE

[Filing a request](#filing-a-request)

[Fee category and waiver](#fee-category-and-waiver)

File with ICE for program-level records. Do *not* expect it to be your fastest route to any individual county's contract documents.

Reference copies of currently-pending ICE FOIAs filed by this guide’s author:

1. [FOIA Request Re: Discrepancy in Publication Currency Data for 287(g) Agreement List](https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vSddyS5y_51flkvXmesEfjc7b_ddc3tzEIM2wCjXOwwRHNpVxbQZKg5sygjhM5aGD-uHUWCh9H9VlWh/pub)  
2. [FOIA Request Re: 287(g) Agreement for Caney Valley Public Schools](https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vTutTaAwRcCzENri-Icrxd0zduFj8uMm24ut3YnKOFVPLimtMT6ZGui4D9mHysai5ChSCWzjzP_Pg4m/pub)

---

## **Filing a request** {#filing-a-request}

287(g) program records — agreements, correspondence about negotiation or cancellation, referral and arrest data, training materials given to participating agencies — are held by ICE, not USCIS. 

[SecureRelease Portal](https://www.securerelease.us/) — preferred. Once you’ve created an account:

1. **Agency:** Department of Homeland Security   
2. **Component:** U.S. Immigration and Customs and Enforcement (ICE)   
3. Scroll down and click  ‘Next’ button  
4. **Select type of requester** (may not be editable for existing SecureRelease profiles)  
5. Scroll down and click ‘Confirm’ button  
6. **Request Details Page:**  
   1. **Request Type:** ‘FOIA Request’  
   2. Paste full request details in ‘**Request Description**’ text field  
   3. **Request Designation**: ‘Other (I am not requesting records about a person)’

**Statutory clock:** 20 business days to respond; 30 where records are in field offices or voluminous.

**Actual timeline:** Commonly 6–18 months or longer for non-expedited institutional requests.

**Appeal window:** 90 days from an adverse determination, to the Office of Principal Legal Advisor, Government Information Law Division, 500 12th St. SW, Stop 5900, Washington, DC 20536-5900.

**Before you file:** 

* Check [ICE's FOIA Library](https://www.ice.gov/foia/library?field_foia_category_target_id=All&combine=287%28g%29&created=&sort_by=created) — some pre-2025 materials are posted there.  
* [SecureRelease Reading Room](https://www.securerelease.us/public-reading-room)

---

## **Fee category and waiver** {#fee-category-and-waiver}

***Fee Waiver Justification:*** As a journalist, you qualify as a news media requester: no search or review fees, and the first 100 pages of duplication free. I recommend stating this explicitly. 

Separately, request a fee waiver on public-interest grounds — describe your outlet/publication, your audience, and how you will publish the released records. The two arguments are independent and may be useful to make together.

---

## **Expedited processing**

Two of the four statutory grounds may fit: urgency to inform the public about federal government activity, where the requester is primarily engaged in disseminating information; and widespread and exceptional media interest affecting public confidence in government. 

# State and local records

[Document custodians](#document-custodians)

[What to ask for](#what-to-ask-for-1)

[Note on constables](#note-on-constables)

Layers 2 through 4 of the 287(g) [document chain](#document-chain) have reached the public almost entirely through county and municipal records requests. This is where your time is particularly valuable in digging into agency-specific contract details.

**Who actually holds it:** The same document may sit in several offices, and you may find less resistance when requesting from an office without a direct stake in the agreement (like a county auditor or board of commissioners).

---

## **Document custodians**  {#document-custodians}

What kinds of records to request from each potential custodian:

**Participating agency:** The service agreement and its attachments, training certifications, officer assignment records, correspondence with ICE.

**Municipal / county auditor, comptroller, etc.:** Invoices, reimbursement requests, payments received, purchase orders, potentially the underlying contract as supporting documentation.

**County commission, city council, etc.:** Meeting agenda packets, minutes, and any resolutions related to or approving the agreement. Agenda attachments are often published online.

**City or county clerk:** Executed contracts, budget amendments or memos re: accepting federal funds.

**State grant administrator (e.g. FL, TX, TN):** Grant applications, award letters, expenditure reports. In [Texas](https://comptroller.texas.gov/economy/development/grants/sb8/) and [Florida](https://myfloridacfo.com/news/pressreleases/press-release-details/2026/07/21/chief-financial-officer-blaise-ingoglia-awards-over--24-million-to-florida-law-enforcement-agencies-to-support-immigration-enforcement), award lists are published.

**State AG or open records office:** Rulings and determinations on prior requests for the same or similar records.

---

## 

## **What to ask for** {#what-to-ask-for-1}

* Name documents, not topics.   
* Ask for the service agreement and all attachments, exhibits, and any riders, addendums, or amendments.  
* Ask separately for invoices and reimbursement requests submitted to ICE or DHS, and for records of payments received.   
* Ask for budget amendments or resolutions accepting the funds, and for purchase orders drawn against them — vehicles, body cameras, software subscriptions.   
* Ask for overtime and travel records for officers assigned to the program, and for out-of-state travel authorizations, which is how the Bradley County constables' multi-state work came to light.   
* Ask for the agenda packet and minutes for the meeting where the agreement was approved.

**Two framing notes:**

1. Request an itemized index of attachments even if you expect the attachments themselves to be withheld — knowing a rider exists is helpful in itself.  
2. Ask for records in native electronic format; agencies that print and scan are often doing so to defeat searchability, reduce general usability, delay release, etc.

---

## **Note on constables** {#note-on-constables}

Pennsylvania, Tennessee, and Texas account for most of the participating constable offices. Constables are independently elected, often operate with minimal administrative infrastructure or oversight, and are unpaid positions in TN \+ PA. 

ICE lists them as municipal agencies, even though their jurisdiction typically covers a segment of a larger county. 

**Consequences for reporting:** 

* population and jurisdiction figures attached to them are unreliable, and often missing in the report.   
* the records custodian may be the constable *personally* rather than a county office — which changes both who you ask and how long it takes.

* [Make the Road Pennsylvania v. Harran](https://www.aclupa.org/cases/make-the-road-pennsylvania-v-harran/) (Bucks County, PA) — ACLU of Pennsylvania and Community Justice Project; trial court ruled for the sheriff on standing; on appeal to Superior Court

  * [outside counsel opinion](https://www.pinal.gov/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/2183) (January 2026\) concluded the office’s agreement was void, absent approval from the county’s Board of Supervisors.

Brad Miller](https://www.pinal.gov/DocumentCenter/View/28488/SuperiorCourtMaricopaCountyFiled5192026) — Maricopa County [superior court judge ruled](https://azmirror.com/2026/05/15/judge-blocks-pinal-county-attorneys-rogue-ice-deal-says-he-exceeded-his-authority/) against Miller’s 287(g) partnership (Arizona Mirror, May 2026).
